lead: An RF power amplifier (PA) is the last active block before the antenna. It must deliver hundreds of milliwatts to many watts while staying linear enough for the modulation. The classes that are most linear waste most of their DC power as heat, and the classes that are most efficient distort the signal and splatter energy into neighbouring channels. Class choice, the load line, back-off and linearisation together set the output power, the battery life and whether the spectral mask is met in handsets, Wi-Fi routers, base stations and radar transmitters.
prereq: You need: compression and IM3, ACLR and PAPR from transmitter architectures, and L-section matching from transmission lines.

blocks.text: The bias point fixes the conduction angle, the part of each RF cycle (in degrees) during which the transistor carries current. Class A conducts for 360° (always on, most linear), Class B for 180° (two devices in push-pull cover the cycle), Class AB between the two (the usual linear handset PA), and Class C for less than 180° (efficient, but the output amplitude no longer follows the input). Classes D, E and F switch the transistor and shape its voltage and current so they do not overlap.

blocks.where: drain (or collector) efficiency; P<sub>out</sub> is the RF output power and P<sub>DC</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>I<sub>DC</sub> the supply power, both in W.
power-added efficiency; P<sub>in</sub> is the RF drive power in W. PAE is always below η<sub>D</sub>, and much below it when the PA gain is low.

blocks.text: For ideal reduced-conduction stages driven to full swing, the maximum efficiency for a conduction angle α (radians) is η = (α − sin α)/[4(sin(α/2) − (α/2)cos(α/2))]. It gives 50 % at 360°, 60.2 % at 270°, 78.5 % (π/4) at 180°, 89.7 % at 120° and 94.0 % at 90°. The output power for the same peak current falls below 180°: by 1.1 dB at 120° and 2.1 dB at 90°.

A choke-fed Class A stage biased at I<sub>DC</sub> = I<sub>max</sub>/2 swings its drain current from 0 to I<sub>max</sub> and its drain voltage from the knee voltage V<sub>knee</sub> to 2V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>knee</sub>. The load that allows both full swings at once is

blocks.where: R<sub>opt</sub> in Ω; voltages in V; I<sub>max</sub> the peak current in A. The output power is P<sub>out</sub> = (V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>knee</sub>)I<sub>max</sub>/4.

blocks.text: This load-line match, not a conjugate match, gives maximum swing rather than maximum gain. R<sub>opt</sub> is usually a few ohms, so a network transforms the 50 Ω load down to it.

Back-off is how far the average output sits below the maximum, BO = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>avg</sub>). The classes lose efficiency at different rates. A Class A stage draws the same DC current at any output, so η falls with the power ratio: η = 50 % × 10<sup>−BO/10</sup>. An ideal Class B stage's DC current falls with the signal amplitude, so η = 78.5 % × 10<sup>−BO/20</sup>. At 6 dB back-off Class A falls to 12.6 % and Class B to 39.4 %. Signals with 8 to 10 dB of PAPR therefore make a plain PA run at a small fraction of its datasheet efficiency.
A nonlinear PA spreads a modulated signal's spectrum (spectral regrowth), raising the adjacent-channel power. Four standard remedies trade complexity for efficiency.

items: Back-off: run the PA far below compression. Simple and linear, but efficiency falls as in the paragraph above.

Digital predistortion (DPD): a baseband block applies the inverse of the PA's nonlinearity before the DAC. A coupler and a feedback receiver sample the PA output so the DPD coefficients can adapt. Memory effects (thermal and bias time constants) make the needed inverse depend on past samples, so DPD uses memory models.

Feedforward: a main PA's output is compared with the clean input, the error is amplified by a separate error amplifier and subtracted at the output through a coupler. It is wideband and very linear, but the error amplifier and couplers waste power, so it is now used mostly where linearity matters more than efficiency.

Doherty and envelope tracking (ET): a Doherty PA has a carrier amplifier and a peaking amplifier joined by a quarter-wave impedance inverter; at low power the peaking amplifier is off and the carrier sees a doubled load, so it reaches full voltage swing (and peak efficiency) 6 dB below maximum. ET makes the supply V<sub>DD</sub>(t) follow the signal envelope, so the voltage across the transistor stays small and little power is lost as heat.

blocks.text: Base stations commonly pair a Doherty PA with DPD; handsets pair ET with DPD.

examples.question: A Class AB PA runs from V<sub>DD</sub> = 3.3 V with an average current of 300 mA. It delivers 250 mW for 50 mW of RF drive. Find P<sub>DC</sub>, the drain efficiency, the PAE and the heat dissipated.
steps: Heat = P<sub>DC</sub> + P<sub>in</sub> − P<sub>out</sub> = 0.990 + 0.050 − 0.250 = 0.790 W, more than three times the RF output.
The PA gain is only 10 log₁₀(250/50) = 7.0 dB, which is why PAE is so far below η<sub>D</sub>.
examples.answer: P<sub>DC</sub> = 0.99 W, η<sub>D</sub> = 25.3 %, PAE = 20.2 %, and 0.79 W becomes heat.

examples.question: Design the output of a 2 GHz Class A PA with V<sub>DD</sub> = 3.3 V, V<sub>knee</sub> = 0.3 V and I<sub>max</sub> = 1 A. Find R<sub>opt</sub>, the output power in W and dBm, the DC power and the efficiency, and the L-section that matches a 50 Ω antenna to R<sub>opt</sub>. What is the efficiency at 6 dB back-off?
steps: Peak voltage swing 3.0 V, peak current swing 0.5 A: P<sub>out</sub> = 3.0 × 0.5/2 = 0.75 W = 10 log₁₀ 750 = 28.8 dBm.
I<sub>DC</sub> = 0.5 A, so P<sub>DC</sub> = 3.3 × 0.5 = 1.65 W and η<sub>D</sub> = 0.75/1.65 = 45.5 % (below 50 % because of V<sub>knee</sub>).
L-section from 50 Ω down to 6 Ω: Q = √(50/6 − 1) = 2.708. Series reactance on the 6 Ω side X<sub>s</sub> = Q × 6 = 16.25 Ω; shunt reactance on the 50 Ω side X<sub>p</sub> = 50/Q = 18.46 Ω.
At 2 GHz (ω = 1.257 × 10¹⁰ rad/s): series L = 16.25/ω = 1.29 nH; shunt C = 1/(ω × 18.46) = 4.31 pF. Check: (6 + j16.25) in parallel with −j18.46 gives 50.0 Ω.
At 6 dB back-off a Class A stage still draws 1.65 W, so η = 45.5 % × 10<sup>−0.6</sup> = 45.5 % × 0.251 = 11.4 %.
examples.answer: R<sub>opt</sub> = 6 Ω, P<sub>out</sub> = 0.75 W (28.8 dBm), P<sub>DC</sub> = 1.65 W, η<sub>D</sub> = 45.5 %; a 1.29 nH series inductor and a 4.31 pF shunt capacitor match 50 Ω to 6 Ω; η falls to 11.4 % at 6 dB back-off.

traps: Quoting the peak efficiency for a modulated signal. At 9 dB back-off a 50 % Class A PA averages 6.3 %.
Equating drain efficiency and PAE. PAE subtracts the drive power; with 7 dB of gain the difference is 5 percentage points in the first worked example.
Conjugate-matching a PA for maximum gain. A PA is matched to R<sub>opt</sub> from its load line, which gives maximum output power.
Using 10<sup>−BO/10</sup> for Class B. Its DC current falls with amplitude, so its efficiency falls as 10<sup>−BO/20</sup>: 39.4 % at 6 dB, not 19.7 %.
Calling Doherty a digital technique. Doherty is load modulation with two amplifiers; DPD is the digital correction.

quiz.q: Define drain efficiency and PAE. Why is PAE lower?
quiz.a: η<sub>D</sub> = P<sub>out</sub>/P<sub>DC</sub>; PAE = (P<sub>out</sub> − P<sub>in</sub>)/P<sub>DC</sub>. PAE takes away the RF drive, which the PA did not add.

quiz.q: Why does Class B reach a higher maximum efficiency than Class A?
quiz.a: Class A draws its full quiescent current all the time, even with no signal. Class B draws current only during the half cycle it conducts, and its average current rises with the signal, so the ideal maximum rises from 50 % to π/4 = 78.5 %.

quiz.q: A PA has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, I<sub>DC</sub> = 0.8 A, P<sub>out</sub> = 2 W and P<sub>in</sub> = 0.2 W. Find P<sub>DC</sub>, η<sub>D</sub> and PAE.
Find the ideal maximum efficiency of a Class C stage with a 120° conduction angle.
Find the Class B efficiency at 6 dB and at 10 dB back-off.

quiz.a: The widening of a modulated signal's spectrum by PA nonlinearity (mostly IM3), which puts power in the adjacent channels and lowers ACLR.

quiz.q: How does a Doherty PA keep its efficiency at 6 dB back-off?
quiz.a: Below 6 dB back-off only the carrier amplifier is on, and the quarter-wave inverter makes it see twice its full-power load, so it reaches full voltage swing at half the current and peak efficiency. Above that the peaking amplifier turns on and pulls the carrier's load back down, so both deliver full power at the peak.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gallium nitride (GaN) transistors dominate base-station and radar PAs for their breakdown voltage and power density. PAs are designed from load-pull measurements, which map output power and efficiency against load impedance. Search for 'load-pull' and 'GaN Doherty amplifier'.

figure.caption: Efficiency falls with back-off at two rates: Class A as the power ratio, Class B as the amplitude ratio. At 6 dB, ideal Class A is down to 12.6 % (the worked example's 45.5 % design to 11.4 %), while ideal Class B still gives 39.4 %.

spec.aria: Drain efficiency in percent against back-off from 0 to 12 dB. The Class B curve starts at 78.5 percent and falls to 39.4 percent at 6 dB. The ideal Class A curve starts at 50 percent and falls to 12.6 percent at 6 dB, and a dashed curve for the worked example's Class A design starts at 45.5 percent and falls to 11.4 percent.
